arXiv:1206.2836v2 [math.AC] 06 Feb 2013

A few remarks on the Generalized Vanishing Conjecture

Michiel de Bondt Note: The author was supported by the Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research (NWO) Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Radboud University Affiliation: Postbus 9010, 6500 GL Nijmegen, The Netherlands Affiliation: E-mail: M.deBondt@math.ru.nl
Abstract

We show that the Generalized Vanishing Conjecture

∀m≥1[Λmfm=0]⟹∀m≫0[Λm(gfm)=0]\forall_{m\geq 1}[\Lambda^{m}f^{m}=0]\Longrightarrow\forall_{m\gg 0}[\Lambda^{m}(gf^{m})=0]

for a fixed differential operator Λ∈k[∂]\Lambda\in k[\partial] follows from a special case of it, namely that the additional factor gg is a power of the radical polynomial ff. Next we show that in order to prove the Generalized Vanishing Conjecture (up to some bound on the degree of Λ\Lambda), we may assume that Λ\Lambda is a linear combination of powers of distinct partial derivatives. At last, we show that the Generalized Vanishing Conjecture holds for products of linear forms in ∂\partial, in particular homogeneous differential operators Λ∈k[∂1,∂2]\Lambda\in k[\partial_{1},\partial_{2}].

Key words: Generalized Vanishing Conjecture, Jacobian Conjecture, differential operator, Weyl algebra.

MSC 2010: 13N10, 14R15, 12H05, 32W99.

Introduction

The Jacobian Conjecture has been the topic of many papers (see [BCW] and [vdE] and its references). Until recently, there was no framework available in which this notorious conjecture could be studied. Based on work in [dBvdE], Wenhua Zhao published several papers ([Zha1], [Zha2], [Zha3], [Zha4]) which have changed this situation dramatically.

In these papers, he introduced various conjectures which imply the Jacobian Conjecture. One of these conjectures is the so-called Generalized Vanishing Conjecture. To describe it, we fix the following notations. Let k⁡[x]=k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x]=k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] be the polynomial ring in nn variables over a field kk. By D=k[∂1,…,∂n]D=k[\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}] we denote the ring of differential operators with constant coefficients. By kk-linearity of taking partial derivative, the following defines Λ​f∈k⁡[x]\Lambda f\in k[x] with Λ∈D\Lambda\in D and f∈k⁡[x]f\in k[x] uniquely:

(Λ1+Λ2)​f\displaystyle(\Lambda_{1}+\Lambda_{2})f =Λ1​f+Λ2​f\displaystyle=\Lambda_{1}f+\Lambda_{2}f (Λ1​Λ2)​f\displaystyle(\Lambda_{1}\Lambda_{2})f =Λ1​(Λ2​f)\displaystyle=\Lambda_{1}(\Lambda_{2}f) ∂if=∂∂xi​f​,\displaystyle\partial_{i}f=\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}f\mbox{,}

where Λ1,Λ2∈D\Lambda_{1},\Lambda_{2}\in D and f∈k⁡[x]f\in k[x].

Generalized Vanishing Conjecture (GVC).

Let Λ∈D\Lambda\in D and f∈k⁡[x]f\in k[x] such that

Λm​fm\displaystyle\Lambda^{m}f^{m} =0​ for all ​m≥1​.\displaystyle=0\mbox{ for all }m\geq 1\mbox{.}
Then for all g∈k⁡[x]g\in k[x], we have
Λm​(g​fm)\displaystyle\Lambda^{m}(gf^{m}) =0​ for all ​m≫0​.\displaystyle=0\mbox{ for all }m\gg 0\mbox{.}

It was shown in [Zha2, Th. 7.2] that for a field kk of characteristic zero, a positive answer to this conjecture (in all dimensions), with Λ\Lambda being the Laplace operator Δ\Delta (and g=fg=f), implies the Jacobian Conjecture. For a field of positive characteristic pp, the GVC can easily be proved, because Λp​g=0\Lambda^{p}g=0 for all Λ∈k[∂]\Lambda\in k[\partial] with trivial constant part and all g∈k⁡[x]g\in k[x].

The main results of this paper can be described as follows. First we show that the gg’s in the formulation of the GVC can be replaced by powers of ff. We will do that in a corollary of the following theorem.

Theorem 1.

Let f~,g∈k⁡[x]\tilde{f},g\in k[x] and m≥dm\geq d. Suppose that

Λm−d​f~=0\displaystyle\Lambda^{m-d}\tilde{f}=0
for some Λ∈D\Lambda\in D. If deg⁡g≤d\deg g\leq d, then
Λm​(g​f~)=0\displaystyle\Lambda^{m}(g\tilde{f})=0

as well.

Corollary 2.

The GVC (for some Λ∈D\Lambda\in D) is equivalent to the following statement: if f∈k⁡[x]f\in k[x] is such that

Λm​fm\displaystyle\Lambda^{m}f^{m} =0​ for all ​m≥1​,\displaystyle=0\mbox{ for all }m\geq 1\mbox{,}
then for each d≥1d\geq 1, we have
Λm​fm+d\displaystyle\Lambda^{m}f^{m+d} =0​ for all ​m≫0​.\displaystyle=0\mbox{ for all }m\gg 0\mbox{.}
Proof.

The statement of corollary 2 follows from the GVC (for Λ∈D\Lambda\in D) by taking g=fdg=f^{d}, so it remains to prove the converse. For that purpose, let g∈k⁡[x]g\in k[x] and choose d≥deg⁡gd\geq\deg g. Combining the condition Λm​fm=0\Lambda^{m}f^{m}=0 for all m≥1m\geq 1 of the GVC (for Λ∈D\Lambda\in D) and the statement of corollary 2, we get Λm​fm+d=0\Lambda^{m}f^{m+d}=0 for all m≫0m\gg 0, which is equivalent to Λm−d​fm=0\Lambda^{m-d}f^{m}=0 for all m≫0m\gg 0. By taking f~=fm\tilde{f}=f^{m} in theorem 1, we subsequently obtain Λm​(g​fm)=0\Lambda^{m}(gf^{m})=0 for all m≫0m\gg 0. ∎

In the proof of [vdEZ, Th. 1.5], corollary 2 is proved for Λ=Δ\Lambda=\Delta, the Laplace operator. The claim of [vdEZ, Th. 1.5] is that one can even take d=1d=1 in corollary 2 when Λ=Δ\Lambda=\Delta, which subsequently follows from (3) ⇒\Rightarrow (2) of [Zha2, Th. 6.2]. Hence we can take g=fg=f in the GVC when we restrict ourselves to Λ=Δ\Lambda=\Delta.

If kk has characteristic zero, then by [Cou, §1.1], we can also formulate theorem 1 and corollary 2 in terms of the nn-th Weyl algebra An​(k)A_{n}(k) over kk. An​(k)A_{n}(k) is the algebra of skew polynomials in xx and ∂\partial over kk, with the following commutator relations, where δ\delta is Kronecker’s delta:

xi​xj−xj​xi\displaystyle x_{i}x_{j}-x_{j}x_{i} =∂i∂j−∂j∂i=0\displaystyle=\partial_{i}\partial_{j}-\partial_{j}\partial_{i}=0 ∂ixj−xj∂i=δi​j\displaystyle\partial_{i}x_{j}-x_{j}\partial_{i}=\delta_{ij} for all ​i,j​.\displaystyle\mbox{ for all }i,j\mbox{.}

We get the Weyl algebra formulation of theorem 1 and corollary 2 as follows. In each of the equalities of the form E=0E=0 in them, we interpret the left hand side EE as an element of An​(k)A_{n}(k), and replace ‘E=0E=0’ by ‘EE is contained in the left ideal of An​(k)A_{n}(k) generated by ∂1,∂2,…,∂n\partial_{1},\partial_{2},\ldots,\partial_{n}’. See [Cou, §5.1] for the justification of this reformulation, especially [Cou, Prop. 5.1.2].

If kk has positive characteristic, then the Weyl algebra formulations of theorem 1 and corollary 2 are not just reformulations of theorem 1 and corollary 2, but really different claims, see [Cou, §2.3]. This is however not essential for the proof of corollary 2, and neither will be essential for the proof of theorem 1 in the next section, so we actually have two theorems 1 and corollaries 2.

Next we show that it suffices to investigate the GVC for a special class of operators. More precisely we show the following.

Theorem 3.

It suffices to investigate the GVC in all dimensions for operators of the form

c1∂1d1+c2∂2d2+⋯+cn∂ndn,c_{1}\partial_{1}^{d_{1}}+c_{2}\partial_{2}^{d_{2}}+\cdots+c_{n}\partial_{n}^{d_{n}}\mbox{,}

where the did_{i} are positive integers and ci∈kc_{i}\in k. Furthermore, we may take ci=1c_{i}=1 or ci2=1c_{i}^{2}=1 for all ii when k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}} or k=ℝk={\mathbb{R}} respectively.

Finally we prove the GVC for the following class of operators.

Theorem 4.

Let Λ∈D\Lambda\in D be a product of linear forms (in the ∂i\partial_{i}). Then the GVC holds for Λ\Lambda.

As a consequence, we can deduce the following.

Corollary 5.

In dimension two, the GVC holds for any homogeneous operator.

Proof.

Assume without loss of generality that kk is algebraically closed. Then any homogeneous polynomial in two variables is a product of linear factors. Hence the result follows from theorem 4. ∎

The proofs

for all g∈k⁡[x]g\in k[x]. By induction on ∑i=1nαi\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}, it follows that [∂α,g]f~[\partial^{\alpha},g]\tilde{f} can be expressed as a kk-linear combination of polynomials of the form Λ∗​(g∗​f~)\Lambda^{*}(g^{*}\tilde{f}), where Λ∗∈D\Lambda^{*}\in D and g∗∈k⁡[x]g^{*}\in k[x] is a polynomial of degree less than deg⁡g\deg g.

Now fix g∈k⁡[x]g\in k[x] as well and set d:=deg⁡gd:=\deg g. If we define D[x](r)​f~D_{[x]}^{(r)}\tilde{f} as the kk-space of polynomials Λ∗​(g∗​f~)\Lambda^{*}(g^{*}\tilde{f}), with Λ∗∈D\Lambda^{*}\in D and g∗∈k⁡[x]g^{*}\in k[x] of degree ≤r\leq r, then [∂α,g]f~∈D[x](d−1)f~[\partial^{\alpha},g]\tilde{f}\in D_{[x]}^{(d-1)}\tilde{f}. Writing an arbitrary operator Λ∈D\Lambda\in D as a kk-linear combination of monomials ∂α\partial^{\alpha}, we deduce that

[Λ,g]​f~∈D[x](d−1)​f~​ for all Λ∈D.[\Lambda,g]\tilde{f}\in D_{[x]}^{(d-1)}\tilde{f}\mbox{ for all $\Lambda\in D$.} (2)
Proof of theorem 1.

Assume deg⁡g≤d\deg g\leq d. Recall that we have Λm−d​f~=0\Lambda^{m-d}\tilde{f}=0 and must show that the left hand side Λm​(g​f~)\Lambda^{m}(g\tilde{f}) of (3) below is zero. If m=dm=d, then f~=0\tilde{f}=0. If d=0d=0, then g∈kg\in k. Hence the cases m=dm=d and d=0d=0 are trivial. So assume that m>d>0m>d>0. Notice that Λ⁡(g​f~)=g⁡(Λ​f~)+[Λ,g]​f~\Lambda(g\tilde{f})=g(\Lambda\tilde{f})+[\Lambda,g]\tilde{f}, whence

Λm​(g​f~)=Λm−1​(g⁡(Λ​f~))+Λm−1​([Λ,g]​f~)​.\Lambda^{m}(g\tilde{f})=\Lambda^{m-1}\big(g(\Lambda\tilde{f})\big)+\Lambda^{m-1}\big([\Lambda,g]\tilde{f}\big)\mbox{.} (3)

Since Λ(m−1)−d​(Λ​f~)=Λm−d​(f~)=0\Lambda^{(m-1)-d}(\Lambda\tilde{f})=\Lambda^{m-d}(\tilde{f})=0, it follows by induction on mm that the first term Λm−1​(g⁡(Λ​f~))=0\Lambda^{m-1}\big(g(\Lambda\tilde{f})\big)=0 on the right hand side of (3) vanishes.

Hence it suffices to show that the second term Λm−1​([Λ,g]​f~)\Lambda^{m-1}\big([\Lambda,g]\tilde{f}\big) on the right hand side of (3) vanishes as well. For that purpose, we use (2) to write [Λ,g]​f~[\Lambda,g]\tilde{f} as a sum of polynomials of the form Λ∗​(g∗​f~)\Lambda^{*}(g^{*}\tilde{f}), where Λ∗∈D\Lambda^{*}\in D and g∗∈k⁡[x]g^{*}\in k[x] such that deg⁡g∗≤d−1\deg g^{*}\leq d-1 for each such term. Thus the second term Λm−1​([Λ,g]​f~)\Lambda^{m-1}\big([\Lambda,g]\tilde{f}\big) on the right hand side of (3) is a sum of polynomials of the form

Λm−1​Λ∗​(g∗​f~)=Λ∗​(Λm−1​(g∗​f~))​,\Lambda^{m-1}\Lambda^{*}(g^{*}\tilde{f})=\Lambda^{*}\big(\Lambda^{m-1}(g^{*}\tilde{f})\big)\mbox{,} (4)

with Λ∗\Lambda^{*} and g∗g^{*} as above. Since Λ(m−1)−(d−1)​(f~)=Λm−d​(f~)=0\Lambda^{(m-1)-(d-1)}(\tilde{f})=\Lambda^{m-d}(\tilde{f})=0, it follows by induction on dd that the second factor on the right hand side of (4) vanishes. So both sides of (3) are zero. ∎

Just as theorem 1 itself, the above proof can be reformulated in terms of the nn-th Weyl algebra An​(k)A_{n}(k) over kk (resulting in the proof of a different theorem when kk has positive characteristic). The Weyl algebra formulation of (1) is [Cou, Exrc. 1.4.1] and the definition of D[x](r)​f~D_{[x]}^{(r)}\tilde{f} corresponds to a filtration which is isomorphic to the order filtration in [Cou, §7.2], see also [Cou, §3.2]. The actual isomorphism is generated by

xi\displaystyle x_{i} ↦∂i\displaystyle\mapsto\partial_{i} ∂i\displaystyle\partial_{i} ↦−xi\displaystyle\mapsto-x_{i} for all ii.

By way of the same isomorphism, it follows from [Cou, Prop. 1.2.1] that every element of An​(k)A_{n}(k) is a linear combination of elements of the form Λ∗​g∗\Lambda^{*}g^{*}, where Λ∗∈D\Lambda^{*}\in D and g∗∈k⁡[x]g^{*}\in k[x]. This fact has some connection with (2).

Proof of theorem 3.

Let Λ∈D\Lambda\in D be a non-zero operator and f∈k⁡[x]f\in k[x] such that Λm​fm=0\Lambda^{m}f^{m}=0 for all m≥1m\geq 1. We must show that Λm​(g​fm)=0\Lambda^{m}(gf^{m})=0 in case the GVC holds for kk-linear combinations of powers of distinct partial derivatives.

  1. i)

    Since each monomial of degree dd appearing in Λ\Lambda can be written as a kk-linear combination of powers of the form ldl^{d}, where ll is a kk-linear combination of ∂1,∂2,…,∂n\partial_{1},\partial_{2},\ldots,\partial_{n}, we can write Λ\Lambda as a kk-linear combination of such powers, i.e.

    Λ=c1​l1d1+c2​l2d2+⋯+cN​lNdN\Lambda=c_{1}l_{1}^{d_{1}}+c_{2}l_{2}^{d_{2}}+\cdots+c_{N}l_{N}^{d_{N}} (5)

    for some ci∈k∗c_{i}\in k^{*}, di∈ℕd_{i}\in{\mathbb{N}}, where li=ai​1∂1+⋯+ai​n∂nl_{i}=a_{i1}\partial_{1}+\cdots+a_{in}\partial_{n}, for some ai​j∈ka_{ij}\in k. If k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}} or k=ℝk={\mathbb{R}}, then we may assume that c1=c2=⋯=cn=1c_{1}=c_{2}=\cdots=c_{n}=1 or c12=c22=⋯=cn2=1c_{1}^{2}=c_{2}^{2}=\cdots=c_{n}^{2}=1 respectively.

  2. ii)

    Now we introduce NN new variables y1,y2,…,yNy_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{N} and consider the operator

    Λ∗:=(∂y1+l1)d1+(∂y2+l2)d2+⋯+(∂yN+lN)dN\Lambda^{*}:=(\partial_{y_{1}}+l_{1})^{d_{1}}+(\partial_{y_{2}}+l_{2})^{d_{2}}+\cdots+(\partial_{y_{N}}+l_{N})^{d_{N}} (6)

    on the polynomial ring k⁡[x1,…,xn,y1,…,yN]k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{N}]. Making the linear coordinate change defined by

    xi′\displaystyle x_{i}^{\prime} :=xi−(a1​i​y1+⋯+aN​i​yN)\displaystyle:=x_{i}-(a_{1i}y_{1}+\cdots+a_{Ni}y_{N}) yj′\displaystyle y_{j}^{\prime} :=yj\displaystyle:=y_{j}

    for all i≤ni\leq n and for all j≤Nj\leq N, we obtain ∂yj+lj=∂yj′\partial_{y_{j}}+l_{j}=\partial_{y_{j}^{\prime}}, because

    (∂yj+lj)xi′\displaystyle(\partial_{y_{j}}+l_{j})x_{i}^{\prime} =−aj​i+aj​i=0\displaystyle=-a_{ji}+a_{ji}=0 (∂yj+lj)yt′\displaystyle(\partial_{y_{j}}+l_{j})y_{t}^{\prime} =δj​t\displaystyle=\delta_{jt}

    for all i≤ni\leq n and all j,t≤Nj,t\leq N. Hence on these new coordinates, the operator Λ∗\Lambda^{*} is of the form as described in the statement of the theorem. It follows that the GVC holds for Λ∗\Lambda^{*}.

  3. iii)

    Since f∈k⁡[x]f\in k[x] satisfies Λm​fm=0\Lambda^{m}f^{m}=0 for all m≥1m\geq 1, it follows from (5) and (6) that also (Λ∗)m​fm=0(\Lambda^{*})^{m}f^{m}=0 for all m≥1m\geq 1. As observed in ii), the GVC holds for Λ∗\Lambda^{*}, thus we obtain that for every g∈k⁡[x]g\in k[x] also (Λ∗)m​(g​fm)=0(\Lambda^{*})^{m}(gf^{m})=0 for all large mm. But again by (5) and (6), it follows that Λm​(g​fm)=0\Lambda^{m}(gf^{m})=0 for all large mm, which concludes the proof. ∎

Finally, we give the proof of theorem 4, in which we re-use some techniques given in the proof of theorem 3.

Proof of theorem 4.

Let Λ=l1⋅l2⋅⋯⋅lN\Lambda=l_{1}\cdot l_{2}\cdot\cdots\cdot l_{N} for some non-zero linear forms lil_{i} in ∂1,∂2,…,∂n\partial_{1},\partial_{2},\ldots,\partial_{n}. As above, introduce NN new variables y1,y2​…,yNy_{1},y_{2}\ldots,y_{N} and consider the operator

Λ∗:=(∂y1+l1)⋅(∂y2+l2)⋅⋯⋅(∂yN+lN)\Lambda^{*}:=(\partial_{y_{1}}+l_{1})\cdot(\partial_{y_{2}}+l_{2})\cdot\cdots\cdot(\partial_{y_{N}}+l_{N}) (7)

Making the linear coordinate change

xi′\displaystyle x_{i}^{\prime} :=xi−(a1​i​y1+⋯+aN​i​yN)\displaystyle:=x_{i}-(a_{1i}y_{1}+\cdots+a_{Ni}y_{N}) yj′\displaystyle y_{j}^{\prime} :=yj\displaystyle:=y_{j}

for all i≤ni\leq n and for all j≤Nj\leq N again, we obtain that on these new coordinates, the operator Λ∗\Lambda^{*} is of the form

∂y1′⋅∂y2′⋅⋯⋅∂yN′.\partial_{y_{1}^{\prime}}\cdot\partial_{y_{2}^{\prime}}\cdot\cdots\cdot\partial_{y_{N}^{\prime}}\mbox{.}

By [vdEWZ, Cor. 3.5.3], it follows that the GVC holds for this operator. Hence the GVC holds for Λ∗\Lambda^{*}. So just as in iii) above, we deduce that the GVC holds for Λ\Lambda. ∎
